name: Phone Addiction Test
tagline: Check how much your smartphone controls your time and mood.
intro: This test looks at four sides of problematic phone use: compulsive checking, restlessness without your phone, the impact on sleep, work and relationships, and using your phone to escape difficult feelings. Answer based on how often each statement has applied to you over the past month. It takes about five minutes and gives you practical ideas to build a healthier relationship with your phone.
seoTitle: Phone Addiction Test: Free smartphone use check
seoDescription: Are you addicted to your phone? Take this free 5-minute test on compulsive use, withdrawal, life impact and escapism and get practical tips.

compulsive_use.name: Compulsive use
compulsive_use.short: How often you check or use your phone automatically, without a clear purpose.
compulsive_use.low: Your answers suggest you mostly use your phone on purpose. You can go long stretches without checking it and stop scrolling when you intend to. This gives you more attention for the people and tasks in front of you. Keep the habits that support this, such as keeping notifications to a minimum. If you notice screen time creeping up during busy or stressful periods, a quick weekly look at your usage statistics will help you stay aware.
compulsive_use.mid: You sometimes pick up your phone on autopilot, especially during pauses, meals or in bed. You are still in control much of the time, but habits may be forming. Try making your phone a little less convenient: move distracting apps off the home screen, switch off non-essential notifications and keep your phone out of the bedroom. Before you unlock it, ask yourself one quick question: what am I picking it up for?
compulsive_use.high: Your answers suggest that checking your phone has become a strong automatic habit. You may unlock it without thinking, scroll far longer than planned and struggle to cut down. This is very common, as many apps are designed to keep you hooked. Start with clear phone-free zones, such as meals and the bedroom, and use grayscale mode or app timers. If you feel unable to change this pattern and it affects your wellbeing, a qualified professional can help you build new habits.

withdrawal.name: Withdrawal
withdrawal.short: How restless, anxious or irritable you feel when you cannot use your phone.
withdrawal.low: Being without your phone does not seem to bother you much. A dead battery, a meeting or a day offline leaves you fairly calm. This is a sign of a relaxed relationship with your device. Keep enjoying phone-free moments, such as walks or hobbies, and protect them. You might even use this ease to model healthy habits for friends or family who find it harder to disconnect.
withdrawal.mid: You feel some unease when your phone is out of reach, such as worrying about missed messages or feeling restless without signal. This is understandable, but it can grow if left unchecked. Practise short, planned breaks: leave your phone in another room for 30 minutes while you read, cook or talk. Gradually extend the time. Noticing that nothing bad happens helps your mind relax about being unreachable.
withdrawal.high: Your answers suggest strong discomfort when you are separated from your phone. You may feel anxious, irritable or lost without it, or feel phantom vibrations. This shows how closely your sense of calm has become tied to your device. Start with very short phone-free periods and slowly lengthen them, using a watch or alarm clock instead of your phone. If this anxiety feels intense or affects your daily wellbeing, a qualified professional can help you work through it.

life_impact.name: Life impact
life_impact.short: How much your phone use affects your sleep, work, health and relationships.
life_impact.low: Your phone use does not seem to get in the way of your daily life. You sleep, work and connect with others without much interference from your screen. That is a healthy balance worth protecting. Keep your screen-free activities, such as exercise, hobbies and face-to-face time, firmly in your week. A periodic check on how you feel after phone use is a simple way to notice if anything starts to change.
life_impact.mid: Your phone sometimes costs you more than you would like: a later bedtime, a distracted conversation or a task left undone. These effects are moderate but worth taking seriously. Pick the area that matters most to you, such as sleep or focus, and set one clear rule, for example no phone after 10 p.m. or phone in a drawer during study time. Small, specific rules work better than vague intentions.
life_impact.high: Your answers suggest your phone use is clearly affecting areas such as sleep, work, health or relationships. You may notice tiredness, falling behind or tension with people close to you. This is a signal to make some changes. Choose two concrete steps, such as charging your phone outside the bedroom and setting app limits during work hours, and ask someone you trust to support you. If it feels hard to change on your own, a qualified professional can help.

escapism.name: Escapism
escapism.short: How much you use your phone to avoid stress, boredom or difficult feelings.
escapism.low: You do not seem to rely on your phone to escape difficult feelings. When you feel stressed, bored or low, you tend to use other ways to cope, such as talking, moving or simply sitting with it. These are valuable skills. Keep nurturing them, and notice which strategies help you most so you can use them on harder days too. Your phone stays a tool rather than a hiding place.
escapism.mid: You sometimes turn to your phone to switch off from stress, boredom or loneliness. A little distraction can be fine, but when it becomes your main way of coping, feelings often return later. Next time you reach for your phone after a tough moment, pause and name what you feel. Then try one alternative first, such as a short walk, a glass of water or a message to a friend.
escapism.high: Your answers suggest your phone has become a main way to escape uncomfortable feelings, worries or tasks. Scrolling may offer quick relief, but it rarely solves what is underneath and can deepen low mood or loneliness over time. Build a short list of other coping options, such as moving, journaling or calling someone, and try one before picking up your phone. If you often feel low, anxious or overwhelmed, talking to a qualified professional can really help.

summary: Your results show four scores from 0 to 100 %. Higher scores mean your phone plays a bigger role in that area. Phones are useful tools, so the question is not whether you use yours, but whether you feel in charge of how you use it. This report is based on your own answers and is not a medical diagnosis.
